Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=0,\,y(0)=y(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1
$$

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be the fundamental solutions, and suppose we define the matrix $A$ as 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

Fill in the correct options in the reasoning below.

$\,$ The boundary value problem has a unique solution if and only if {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The fundamental solutions to this BVP are {{field-2}}.

$\,$ For this BVP, we have $det(A)=$ {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Therefore, this BVP {{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ 

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=1,{\beta }_{i}=0,a=0,$ and $b=1,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-m-2 & =0 \\ (m-2)(m+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=2$ and $m=-1,$ and so the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x}\text{ and }{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ {e}^{2} & {e}^{-1}\end{aligned}]
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & ={e}^{-1}-{e}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{e}-{e}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}(x)+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0,
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ 

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$
In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Robin boundary conditions, given by

$$
y(0)+{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(1)-{y}^{′}(1)=0.
$$

So, setting ${\alpha }_{1}=1,$ ${\beta }_{1}=1,$ ${\alpha }_{2}=1,$ ${\beta }_{2}=-1,$ and $a=0,$  $b=1,$ the matrix $A$ becomes

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0)+{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}(0)+{y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1)-{y}_{1}^{′}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)-{y}_{2}^{′}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-3m+2 & =0 \\ (m-1)(m-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have ${m}_{1}=1$ and ${m}_{2}=2,$ and so the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}\,\text{and}\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=2{e}^{2x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{0}+{e}^{0} & {e}^{3(0)}+2{e}^{2(0)} \\ {e}^{1}-{e}^{1} & {e}^{2(1)}-2{e}^{2(1)}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -{e}^{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =2(-{e}^{2})-0(3) \\  & =-2{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has a unique solution }y≡0.$

questions.problem:
Consider the following boundary value problem.

$$
{y}^{″}-y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)-y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)-y(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1
$$

Find the solution to this boundary value problem in terms of an arbitrary constant $A.$

The solution is $y=A\,\cdot $
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To solve the homogeneous boundary value problem, we first find the general solution and then determine the values of the arbitrary constants that fit the boundary conditions.

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 1.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-x}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}^{′}=A{e}^{x}-B{e}^{-x}.
$$

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(0)-y(0)=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-B-(A+B) & =0 \\ -2B & =0 \\ B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
y=A{e}^{x}.
$$

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(1)-y(1)=0,$ we have

$$
A{e}^{1}-A{e}^{1}=0,
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $A.$

Therefore, the solution to the BVP is

$$
y=A\cdot {e}^{x},
$$

where $A$ is arbitrary.

$$
{y}^{″}+y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}
$$

Find the solution to this boundary value problem in terms of an arbitrary constant $A.$

The solution is $y=A\,\cdot $
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To solve the homogeneous boundary value problem, we first find the general solution and then determine the values of the arbitrary constants that fit the boundary conditions.

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm \text{i}.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}^{′}=-A\operatorname{sin}⁡x+B\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0,$ we have

$$
-A\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0\,⇒\,B=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Applying the condition $y(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ we have

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $A.$

Therefore, the solution to the BVP is $y=A\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ where $A$ is arbitrary.

questions.problem:
Consider the following boundary value problem.

$$
{y}^{″}=0,\,y(-2)=0,\,y(2)-4{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,-2\le x\le 2
$$

Find the solution to this boundary value problem in terms of an arbitrary constant $A.$

The solution is $y=A\,\cdot ($
{{field-1}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve the homogeneous boundary value problem, we first find the general solution and then determine the values of the arbitrary constants that fit the boundary conditions.

We have the equation

$$
{y}^{″}(x)=0.
$$

Integrating this equation twice, we get the general solution

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}^{′}=A.
$$

Applying the condition $y(-2)=0,$ we have

$$
-2A+B=0\,⇒\,B=2A.
$$

So, we have

$$
y=Ax+2A=A(x+2).
$$

Applying the condition $y(2)-4{y}^{′}(2)=0,$ we have

$$
4A-4A=0
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $A.$

Therefore, the solution to the BVP is $y=A\cdot (x+2),$ where $A$ is arbitrary.

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions.  So, setting $\alpha_i=0,$ $\beta_i=1,$ $a=1,$ and $b=3,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067309/assets/91f85685d5a17221398842923709c20b0e296e53fedb30ee6a4fdcb16d99e0d8.png)

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y=e^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-2m-3 & =0 \\ (m-3)(m+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=3$ and $m=-1,$ and so the fundamental solutions are

$$
y_{1}(x)=e^{3x}\;\textrm{and}\;y_{2}(x)=e^{-x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
y_1'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad y_2'(x) = -e^{-x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3(1)} & -{e}^{-1} \\ 3{e}^{3(3)} & -{e}^{-3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3} & -{e}^{-1} \\ 3{e}^{9} & -{e}^{-3}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(3{e}^{3})(-{e}^{-3})-(-{e}^{-1})(3{e}^{9}) \\  & =-3+3{e}^{8} \\  & =3({e}^{8}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A)\ne0,$ we conclude that this BVP has the unique trivial solution $y\equiv0.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Homogeneous BVPs With Nontrivial Solutions
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following boundary value problem.

$$
y'' = 0, \qquad y(4) = 0, \quad y(3) + y'(3) = 0,\quad 3\leq x \leq 4
$$

Find the solution to this boundary value problem in terms of an arbitrary constant $A.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To solve the homogeneous boundary value problem, we first find the general solution and then determine the values of the arbitrary constants that fit the boundary conditions.

We have the equation

$$
y''(x) = 0.
$$

Integrating this equation twice, we get the general solution

$$
y = Ax + B.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
y' = A.
$$

Applying the condition $y(4) = 0,$ we have

$$
4A + B = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad B = -4A.
$$

So, we have

$$
y = Ax - 4A = A(x-4).
$$

Applying the condition $y(3) + y'(3) = 0,$ we have

$$
-A+A = 0,
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $A.$

Therefore, the solution to the BVP is $y = A\cdot \left(x-4\right),$
where $A$ is arbitrary.
